records.our_prose: This is the most important thing about growing apples: one apple tree on its own usually will not make fruit. Apple flowers need pollen from a different apple variety, carried over by bees. So plan to plant two different kinds of apple, not two of the same, within about 50 ft of each other, and make sure they bloom at the same time (an early bloomer cannot help a late bloomer). If you only have room for the idea of one tree, a flowering crabapple planted nearby can do the pollinating job instead. Golden Delicious is a reliable all-around partner that pollinates almost any apple. A few special varieties (Mutsu, Jonagold, Shizuka) cannot pollinate anything and actually need two other partners themselves, so ask the nursery if a variety is "triploid" before you rely on it as your second tree.

Best where space is tight and early fruit and easy picking matter more than tree vigor.

records.our_prose: If your tree comes bare-root (bare roots, no pot), plant it in late winter or early spring while it is still leafless and dormant, as soon as you can dig the soil. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough that the roots can spread out without folding. The key thing: find the graft union (the bumpy spot low on the trunk where the top variety was joined to the roots) and keep it about 2 to 3 in above the soil, never bury it. Fill the hole with the same soil you dug out, water well, and tie small trees to a stake. A potted tree is planted the same way and can go in anytime through spring.

records.our_prose: Plant a bare-root tree while fully dormant, late winter to early spring, as soon as the ground is workable. Soak the roots in water for an hour or two before planting, dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending, and set the tree so the graft union (the swollen knob where the variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 in above the final soil line, burying it defeats the dwarfing rootstock by letting the variety root over. Backfill with native soil, water in to settle, and stake dwarf stocks (M9, M26) permanently. A potted tree follows the same depth rule but can go in through spring.
